newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD-Attention on Bundesbank, French budget.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Attention on Bundesbank, French budget.

text.p: Germany and France will provide the main focus for financial markets in the week ahead with the Bundesbank reconvening after its summer break and talks expected to continue on the key 1998 French budget, analysts said on Friday.
"The Bundesbank council meeting will dominate European trading far in advance of any of the data that is coming out," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London.

The mark's strength has fanned speculation of a near-term rise in German rates, but economists believe German data out in the coming week will make clear a move is unlikely at Thursday's Bundesbank meeting.
In the United States, the Federal Open Market Committee is due to meet on Tuesday but few analysts were anticipating a change in monetary policy.
"There is a virtual consensus that they are not going to move," Fishwick said.
With regards to economic data, it will be a lean week. The main focus will be German July M3 data -- due between Tuesday and Friday -- and British July retail sales, set for release on Wednesday.
Analysts said U.S. June international trade data, also due Wednesday, would be of some interest.
But the markets are gripped by speculation the Bundesbank will opt for an early interest rate rise.
"We ultimately think that speculation will be wrong and that they will probably raise in September at some point," said Fishwick.
Robert Prior, European economist at HSBC James Capel in London said there had been talk that German rates would be on hold until its repo tender the following week.
"But, if Germany does raise rates more than 0.1 percent then France will follow," he said.
The Bank of France will also hold its regular policy meeting on Thursday, while talks for the 1998 budget were expected to get going again at the cabinet meeting on Wednesday.

The budget will be key to showing France's commitment to a single currency and to determining the strength of the European single currency. The country's 1997 GDP/deficit ratio is currently estimated above the three percent EMU target, at 3.5 to 3.7 percent.

"The budget talks are very important," said Prior. "France has to put in place structured measures instead of the one off contributions such as France Telecom. But given the noises we've been hearing about one-offs from electricity companies and savings banks, we're not hugely hopeful they will tackle the problem."

Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London said among the economic data releases German July M3, due between Tuesday and Friday, and the Ifo business climate index on Wednesday would be key.
"M3 will be important because the Bundesbank highlighted it in the monthly report," he said.

In June M3 grew at a seasonally-adjusted, annualised rate of 6.4 percent compared with the fourth quarter of 1996. A Reuters poll of 10 analysts in Germany showed that many were expecting M3 growth for July to slow to between 6.2 and 6.3 percent.
In Britain analysts said attention was centred on July retail sales and provisional M4 data for clues to whether the recent boom in consumer spending will continue.
Average market forecasts predict a month-on-month increase of 0.4 percent in retail sales, slightly slower than the 0.6 percent rise seen in June.
"The retail sales are probably the most important numbers at the moment so to that extent they will be a major focus," Schmidt said.
"UK retail sales are difficult (to predict) because we have had two strong months and some people might be looking for a bit of a dip. I suspect people will be looking for about 0.4," said Schmidt.
